scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Thanksgiving is next week and I'm responsible for preparing the turkey for the first time. My family has a specific recipe for it that everyone expects. How would you approach that?

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared. prediction.raw: This is a **complex and emotionally charged** scenario, and whether you were "AITA" depends on perspective, intent, and the broader context of your relationship with your mother. Here’s a nuanced breakdown of the ethical and relational dimensions: --- ### **Why Some Would Say You Were AITA (Score: ~0)** 1. **Emotional Cruelty**: - You **directly linked her divorce to your dress choice**, which is a painful and personal connection for her. Even if it’s true, framing it as a reason ("*because you wore white and got divorced*") is emotionally brutal. It’s like saying, "Your failure is why I reject something you love." This isn’t about the dress—it’s about **wounding her**. - Her reaction (crying) suggests this hit a nerve. Divorce is a deep, unresolved wound for many, and revisiting it—even indirectly—can feel like reopening old scars. 2. **Lack of Empathy**: - You **prioritized your preferences** over her feelings, even when she was clearly upset. You could have said: - *"I don’t want white, but I love you and don’t want to hurt you. Let’s find a dress that makes us both happy."* - *"I’m choosing a colored dress because I like the style, and I’d love to shop with you—maybe we can find something that feels special to both of us."* - Instead, you **digged in your heels** ("*it’s my wedding, I get to pick*"), which shut down collaboration. 3. **Justifying Your Choice**: - You **avoided owning your real reason** (her divorce) until forced to, which made the conversation feel manipulative. If you’d said upfront: *"I don’t want white because it feels tied to a tradition I don’t believe in, and I’d rather start fresh with something that feels uniquely mine."* —that would have been honest but **not accusatory**. 4. **Power Dynamics**: - You **used your role as the daughter** to assert control over a shared tradition (family dress colors). While it’s your wedding, her feelings matter too. A healthier approach would have been: *"I’d love to honor our family’s tradition, but I’m drawn to a different color. Can we find a compromise?"* --- ### **Why Some Would Say You Were *Not* AITA (Score: ~1)** 1. **It *Is* Your Wedding**: - You’re **entitled to personal preferences**, especially if you’ve already researched and decided. The shop only carried white, and you had valid reasons (aesthetic, cultural, or personal) for rejecting it. **You weren’t wrong to say no.** 2. **Her Reaction Was Overblown**: - Her divorce is **her story to tell**, not yours to weaponize. While your phrasing was harsh, her emotional response might have been **projected guilt**—she may have internalized blame for the divorce and reacted defensively when you challenged her choices. 3. **You Tried to Compromise (Sort Of)**: - You **didn’t outright refuse** to shop with her; you just said the shop didn’t fit your style. A better follow-up could have been: *"Let’s find another shop where we can both find something beautiful!"* —but you didn’t, which left her feeling dismissed. 4. **You’re Not the Villain**: - You’re **not responsible for her divorce**, nor are you obligated to make her feel better about it. However, **how you communicated** made it feel like you were. --- ### **The Ethical Gray Area** This falls into the **"right to autonomy vs. kindness"** dilemma. You had every right to choose a colored dress, but **how you delivered the message** crossed into cruelty. The key difference between "AITA" and "not AITA" here is **intent and empathy**: - **AITA**: If you **meant to hurt her** (even subconsciously) by tying her divorce to your dress. - **Not AITA**: If you **genuinely believed your choice was valid** and just **failed to communicate with care**. --- ### **How to Repair This** 1. **Apologize Sincerely**: - *"I realize now how much that conversation hurt you, and I shouldn’t have brought up your divorce. I love you, and I should have handled this with more care. I’m sorry."* - **Don’t justify further**—just own it. 2. **Reaffirm Your Relationship**: - *"I want us to find a dress that feels special to both of us. Let’s make this a joyful experience, not a source of tension."* 3. **Find a Compromise**: - If she still wants to shop together, suggest a **different bridal shop** where colored dresses are available. If she’s still upset, give her space to process. 4. **Address the Underlying Issue**: - If her divorce is a **repeated sore spot**, you might gently say: *"I know this is hard for you to talk about. I love you, and I’d never want to make you feel bad about your choices."* --- ### **Final Verdict: ~0.5 (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong, But Clearly Improvable)** You **had the right to choose a colored dress**, but **how you communicated it was unkind and unnecessarily confrontational**. The fact that you’re **already feeling guilty** suggests you recognize this wasn’t your best moment. **Repairing the relationship** (with an apology and compromise) is the next step. Would you like help drafting an apology message to her? Or strategies for finding a dress that honors both your preferences and her feelings?
